descriptions: the one unconditioned dhamma among the four ultimate realities (citta, cetasika, rūpa, nibbāna)
single in its own nature (sabhāva) but described as with residue (sa-upādisesa) and without residue (anupādisesa), and as empty, signless and desireless
an object (ārammaṇa) of the path and fruition consciousness, not a mere absence
negations: not arisen, not ageing, not dying (asaṅkhata)
not a self: 'there is extinction, but no one extinguished' (Vism XVI, PTS p. 513)
relation_to_self: no self is found in or behind it; all dhammas including nibbāna are not-self
relation_to_world: the cessation of the conditioned; entirely transcending the world of the five aggregates
caveat: The commentarial tradition would reject any reading of nibbāna as a cosmic ground, a creator or a self; the 'one truth' reading applies only in the sense that nibbāna is the single unconditioned element.

descriptions: the unconditioned ultimate reality of the Abhidhamma, to be realized in this very life by insight developed through the thirty-seven requisites of awakening
relation_to_self: no self; the belief in self (sakkāya-diṭṭhi) is the first thing to be removed
relation_to_world: the cessation of the round of rebirth
caveat: Ledi's writings keep to the commentarial Abhidhamma: nibbāna is not a ground of being or a self.

descriptions: the ultimate truth beyond mind and matter, experienced when the arising and passing of sensations is fully penetrated and all saṅkhāras are eradicated
described in courses as the stage beyond the field of mind and matter, where nothing arises
relation_to_self: the 'I' is a mass of vibrations arising and passing; no permanent self
relation_to_world: the world of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) is experienced as constantly arising and passing; nibbāna is beyond it
caveat: Presented as a universal law of nature (dhamma) rather than as a theology; the tradition would reject speculation about the ultimate in place of practice.

descriptions: experienced at the path and fruition moments as the cessation of all formations noted up to that point; afterwards it can be re-entered as fruition attainment
relation_to_self: noting reveals only arising and passing processes, no self who notes
relation_to_world: the cessation of the noted object and the noting mind
caveat: The tradition describes nibbāna by the knowledges leading to it, not as a metaphysical ground.

descriptions: reached by unbroken mindfulness of touch and feeling when sensation, including pain, is penetrated and ends
caveat: The Sunlun teaching speaks little about the ultimate in abstract terms; entry kept minimal.

descriptions: the unconditioned element, object of the path and fruition knowledges, realized after the ultimate realities of mentality-materiality and their causes have been directly seen
relation_to_self: only mentality-materiality and their causes are found; no being or self
caveat: Follows the Visuddhimagga's account strictly; no ground-of-being reading.

descriptions: the heart released from all defilements, known directly by the one who has reached it
Ajahn Maha Boowa: the 'pure citta' after even the radiant point of the mind — the seat of ignorance — has been destroyed; it does not die
Ajahn Chah: the unconditioned is realized by letting go; 'peace' beyond happiness and suffering
relation_to_self: the teachers deny that the released heart is a self, yet speak of it in positive terms (pure, deathless), a feature noted by other traditions
relation_to_world: beyond the conventions (sammuti) of the world, while conventions are still used
caveat: The forest teachers would reject a reading of the released citta as an ātman or a cosmic self; they speak from their practice, not as metaphysics.

descriptions: the coolness of the extinction of defilements, available here and now, momentarily (tadaṅga-nibbāna) and finally
the mind void of 'I' and 'mine' (chit wang)
relation_to_self: nibbāna is the complete absence of the illusion of 'I' and 'mine'
relation_to_world: not a place or a heaven after death; found in the midst of life
caveat: Buddhadāsa described Dhamma, God and nature in parallel terms in dialogue with other religions, but denied a personal creator; the one-truth reading is a reconciliation he partly invited.

descriptions: the goal of the sequential installation of meditative qualities in the body, reached through the path and fruit
caveat: Very little of the tradition's own discursive statements on the ultimate is available; entry minimal and low confidence.

descriptions: the Dhammakāya, a luminous Buddha-form, is found within at the body's centre
nibbāna described as a true self (attā) and as a realm (āyatana) where the Buddhas abide (the tradition's teaching)
relation_to_self: teaches a true self in nibbāna, distinct from the non-self aggregates
relation_to_world: the refined inner bodies lead beyond the world
caveat: Mainstream Thai Theravāda scholars (notably P. A. Payutto) reject the teaching that nibbāna is a self; recorded as a dispute (dsp:nibbana-atta-or-anatta).

descriptions: the cessation of the round of dependent origination, reached by seeing the arising and passing of consciousness and feeling
caveat: Low confidence; no primary text read.
